desc:
6 Signs You're More Attractive Than You Think (Men)

In 2018, researchers at Cornell and Harvard ran a very simple study. They had strangers talk to each other for a few minutes, then asked two questions. How much did you like them. And how much do you think they liked you. The gap between those two answers was large, consistent, and in the same direction for almost everyone. People liked each other far more than either of them realized. They called it the liking gap. This video is about six signs that gap is happening to you right now, and why the sixth one has almost nothing to do with your face.

📌 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
✓ Why you systematically misjudge how much people like you
✓ What a quick look away actually means
✓ Why people act strange and awkward around you
✓ The small favors strangers do without knowing why
✓ Why people start copying your posture
✓ What genuinely changes how good looking you seem to others

⏱️ CHAPTERS:
0:00 Intro
0:43 The Gap
1:39 Look Away
2:30 Awkward
3:23 Favors
4:03 Mimicry
4:47 What Changes
6:39 Close

🧠 THE SCIENCE:
Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom and Clark in 2018 found a consistent liking gap. After conversations, people underestimated how much their partner liked them, and the effect persisted across settings and over months. Chartrand and Bargh in 1999 demonstrated the chameleon effect, showing that people unconsciously copy the posture and gestures of others, and that this mimicry increases with liking. Moreland and Beach in 1992 had women attend a university lecture a different number of times without speaking to anyone, and the ones who attended most were rated as more attractive by students who had never spoken to them. And Lewandowski, Aron and Gee in 2007 found that information about someone personality measurably changed how physically attractive people rated their face.

💡 KEY TAKEAWAY:
You are not seeing what they see. And most of what they see is not your face.

📚 RESEARCH MENTIONED:
• Boothby, E. J., Cooney, G., Sandstrom, G. M., & Clark, M. S. (2018). The liking gap in conversations. Psychological Science.
• Chartrand, T. L., & Bargh, J. A. (1999). The chameleon effect: The perception behavior link and social interaction. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
• Moreland, R. L., & Beach, S. R. (1992). Exposure effects in the classroom. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.
• Lewandowski, G. W., Aron, A., & Gee, J. (2007). Personality goes a long way: The malleability of opposite sex physical attractiveness. Personal Relationships.

This video is for education and self-reflection. It is not therapy or relationship counseling.

vo: In 2018, researchers at Cornell and Harvard ran a study so simple it almost sounds like nothing. They had strangers talk for a few minutes, then asked each of them two questions. How much did you like them. And how much do you think they liked you. The gap between those answers was large, it was consistent, and it pointed the same way for almost everyone. Everyone liked everyone else more than either of them realized. They called it the liking gap. So here are six signs it is happening to a man right now. And the sixth one has almost nothing to do with his face. One. You are a bad judge of your own effect. Here is the thing to sit with. The man did not misjudge slightly. He misjudged in a direction, and he does it every single time. In the study, the effect did not disappear with time. It showed up after short conversations, and it was still there months later between people who had become friends. The reason is mechanical, not emotional. You hear your own thoughts, which are mostly critical. You only see their face, which is mostly polite. So you compare a hundred of your worst internal moments against one of their most controlled external ones, and then call the result an honest assessment. It is not honest. It is the one judgement you are structurally guaranteed to get wrong, and you have been trusting it for years. Two. The quick look away. She looks at the man. He looks back. She immediately looks away. And every man reads this the same wrong way. He thinks it means she was not looking, or she got caught doing something she did not want to do, or she was unimpressed. Indifference does not produce speed. When someone genuinely does not care, their eyes pass over you and keep going, slowly, like you are a wall. Speed means something registered. The nervous system reacted before the thinking part had a chance to arrange a calm face. So the quick look away is not a verdict. It is a reaction. Those are very different pieces of information, and the man has been filing them in the wrong folder. Three. People get strange around you. Someone talks too fast around the man. Someone else goes quiet. Someone laughs a half second too long at something that was not that funny. The brain files all of that under something is wrong with me. There is another reading, and it fits the evidence better. People are not awkward around people they feel nothing about. Neutral is easy. Neutral is the most comfortable state there is. Awkwardness takes effort. It is what happens when someone is monitoring themselves, and people only monitor themselves in front of someone whose opinion has weight. That is the whole sign. Strangeness around a man is not a sign he is unwelcome. It is a sign he is being taken seriously by someone who did not plan to. Four. The small unexplained favors. Someone holds a door a second longer. A barista remembers the order. A colleague says yes to something they say no to for everyone else. People explain these to themselves afterwards. They say they were in a good mood, or they had time, or it was nothing. The explanation comes after the behavior. Liking moves the hands before it reaches the words, and most people never catch themselves doing it. So the man should stop counting compliments, which almost nobody gives, and start counting small effort, which almost everybody gives away without meaning to. Five. They start moving like you. In 1999, Chartrand and Bargh documented something they called the chameleon effect. People unconsciously copy the posture, gestures and speech rhythm of whoever they are with. And crucially, the copying increases with liking. The more someone likes you, the more their body drifts toward matching yours. So watch the arms. If the man crosses his and the person across from him crosses theirs within a minute, that is not a coincidence and neither of them chose it. It works in reverse too, which is the useful part. Lean back and relax, and watch how many people in the room exhale with you. Six. What actually changes it. Here is the sign that is not a sign. It is a mechanism, and it is the reason the other five are even possible. In 1992, Moreland and Beach had four women attend a large university lecture a different number of times. Fifteen times, ten, five, or never. They spoke to no one. At the end of term, students rated them. The women who had attended most were rated as more attractive. No one had ever spoken to them. That is the mere exposure effect. Familiarity itself changes how a face is read, before a single word is exchanged. And in 2007, Lewandowski and his colleagues went further. They gave people information about someone personality and then asked them to rate the same photograph. The ratings of the exact same face moved. Not slightly. Enough to matter. What people knew about the person changed what they saw in the picture. So the face is the frame. What fills it is how a man speaks, how he treats people when nothing is at stake, and whether being near him is easy. And this is where the liking gap and the attraction research meet, because they are describing the same machine from two ends. People are reading a whole person while the man is auditing a single photograph. He has been grading himself on the one part of the picture that barely moves, and ignoring every part that moves constantly. Which is also why the advice to just be confident fails. Confidence is not a face you make. It is what is left when a man stops running an audit nobody asked for. What to do with this. Now the honest part, because this video could easily become a comfortable lie and I do not want to hand you one. Being more attractive than you think is not the same as being attractive to everyone. The liking gap is a correction, not a promotion. And none of this means the man should stop. Sleep, training, a haircut that fits his head and clothes that fit his body still matter and always will. The point is narrower than that. The part you have been failing at is probably not the part you think, because you have been auditing the wrong thing. And if you want one sentence to take away from all six, it is this. The man has been solving for the wrong variable, and solving it very hard for a very long time. You are not seeing what they see. And most of what they see is not your face. So here is a task. This week, count the small favors instead of the compliments. Come back and tell me the number. And if people act strange around you a lot, the next video explains exactly what that is. Watch that one.
